title: Effects of Heat Treatment on the Microstructural Morphology of Additively Manufactured 316L Stainless Steel
content: 316L Stainless steel (SS) is widely utilized across various industries, particularly in corrosive environments such as marine, chemical, biomedical, and nuclear energy sectors. In recent years, selective laser melting (SLM) has been increasingly employed to fabricate structural components with complex geometries, enhanced mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance [1]. SLM is a powder bed fusion method that utilizes lasers to selectively fuse powdered materials within a confined chamber [2]. The aim of this research is to study the effects of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical properties of selective laser melted (SLMed) 316L stainless steel with time and temperature. In this study, a SLM 125 3D-printer was used to fabricate 316L SS square plates in a 90 ° build orientation. Specimens were then extracted from these plates and subjected to various tests. These specimens were subjected to varying heat treatments using a Thermcraft XSB box furnace at 600 °C for 2 hours (HT1), 600 °C for 6 hours (HT2), and 850 °C for 2 hours (HT3). After heat treatment, the specimens were cooled in an ambient environment. A LECO LM 100 micro-hardness tester with an applied force of 0.2 kgf for 30 s was used to carry out Vickers hardness testing on metallographically prepared samples which were extracted from the Z-plane. The diagonals of the indentations generated by the micro-hardness tester were measured to calculate the hardness of specimens subjected to each heat treatment as well as the as-printed (AP) specimen. Vertical (parallel to build orientation) and horizontal (perpendicular to build orientation) rectangular specimens were extracted from the 3D-printed 316L SS plates. These specimens had average dimensions of 2.78 mm in thickness, 11.52 mm in width, and 50.80 mm in gauge length. An 810-material test system (MTS) was used to carry out tensile testing on these samples. For the microstructural analysis, samples were taken from as-printed and heat-treated specimens in the XY (top down view) and Z (side view) plane. These samples were metallographically prepared, etched with aqua regia (3:1 mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid), and analyzed with an Olympus DSX 1000 Digital Microscope. A Hitachi S3400N scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to examine the specimens subjected to microhardness testing, and they were also metallographically prepared and etched with aqua regia solution.
